title: Finding Extreme Values Without Inventing Data

blocks.text: The minimum needs a real data point

The smallest and largest elements describe values that actually occur in a collection. They do not exist in an empty collection. For a nonempty collection, we can initialize menor and mayor with the first element and update them as we visit other elements. We do not choose zero by habit: zero may not be present and could produce the wrong result when all values are positive or negative.
Both summaries begin with actual values from the collection. Visiting the first element again does not change them; using the same body for all elements keeps the traversal simple.
The property maintained at every step

After each visit, menor is the minimum of the elements seen so far and mayor is their maximum. If the new value is smaller than the previous minimum, it replaces it; otherwise, that minimum remains correct. The same reasoning applies to the maximum, using the opposite comparison.

blocks.text: The nonempty branch gives menor and mayor a clear scope: they exist only when the collection has elements. We do not try to use these names afterward to represent a result that might never have been computed.
An extreme value versus its position

Finding the smallest value does not yet tell us where it appeared. If we also need its first position, we traverse indices and change the stored position only when the value is strictly smaller than the previous best. A tie does not replace the first match. Each access remains protected by a nonempty collection and the condition i < size().

blocks.text: Build and test cases that expose mistakes

Build a report for {4, 9, 2}: print Minimum: 2 and Maximum: 9 on separate lines. For an empty collection, print No data. Repeat with {0}, {-6}, {-7, -3, -5}, {5, 5}, and {8, 2, 8}. Write the expected results before running the program and explain how the initial extremes are chosen without assuming zero belongs to the data.

As a follow-up, add the first position of the minimum only inside the nonempty branch. Use a collection with a repeated minimum to check the tie-breaking rule. We will not reorder the data to solve this lab.
